While line 9 attempts to block forks, an attacker can open a PR from a branch in the main repo (if they have any write access) or the check could be bypassed. This is a known dangerous pattern that has led to supply chain attacks. For publishing on merge, use 'push' trigger with 'branches: [main]' instead.

Scope violation: PR description says 'publish images on merge' but pull_request_target triggers on PR open/update, NOT on merge. This will attempt to publish on every PR push, contradicting the stated purpose. Use 'on: push: branches: [main]' to publish after merge.

The fork check uses negation of a property that may not exist on non-fork PRs, which could cause unexpected behavior. More robust: 'github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository' but this entire trigger pattern should be replaced per blocking findings.

runs_detail.summary: Critical security issue: workflow triggers on pull_request_target from untrusted PRs with write permissions, creating a privilege escalation vector. The fork check is insufficient protection.

findings.comment: Security: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to secrets, even for PRs from forks. Combined with packages:write permission (line 7) and REGISTRY_TOKEN secret (line 15), this allows any external contributor to publish arbitrary images to your registry by opening a PR. The fork check on line 9 does not prevent this — pull_request_target executes workflow code from the base branch, but the PR author controls what gets built/published through the PR changes. This is a well-documented GitHub Actions security anti-pattern for publish workflows.

For merge-time publishing, use 'push: branches: [main]' or 'pull_request: types: [closed]' with a merged check.
